content.ref_size: Set the canvas window size in pixels.
content.ref_size_advanced: Usually called once at the top of your script before any drawing. Calling it later resizes the canvas; subsequent draws use the new dimensions. Floats are accepted but stored as ints. The Window singleton exposes the same as Window.size(w, h).
content.ref_width: Returns the current canvas width in pixels.
content.ref_width_advanced: Reflects the current size — if you call size() to resize, width() returns the new value. Cheap to call every frame; use it for responsive layout instead of hard-coding pixel values. Same as Window.width.
content.ref_height: Returns the current canvas height in pixels.
content.ref_height_advanced: Reflects the current size after size() calls. Pair with width() to position things relative to the canvas. Same as Window.height.
content.ref_background: Clear the canvas. Accepts a color name, an RGB tuple from Colors, or three numbers 0–255. Example: background("black") or background(Colors.blue).
content.ref_background_advanced: If you pass a loaded sprite asset (e.g. `assets.sprites.sky`) instead of a color, the sprite is *stretched* to fill the canvas — useful for parallax/skybox backdrops. The sprite must be fully loaded (`done=True`); a not-yet-loaded asset is silently ignored.
content.ref_background_param_color: Color name, Colors.* tuple, a gray value, or r, g, b components.
content.ref_circle: Draw a filled circle centered at (x, y) with the given radius.
content.ref_rect: Draw a filled rectangle. The top-left corner is at (x, y).
content.ref_ellipse: Draw a filled ellipse centered at (x, y). Omit h to draw a circle.
content.ref_line: Draw a line between two points.
content.ref_point: Draw a single dot at position (x, y).
content.ref_text: Draw a string. Pass an x, y position for manual placement, or an AnchorPoint (e.g. Window.top_right, actor.top) for automatic edge alignment with padding.
content.ref_text_param_x: X position (when not using an anchor).
content.ref_text_param_y: Y position (when not using an anchor).
content.ref_text_param_anchor: A Window or actor anchor. Sets alignment and padding automatically.
content.ref_say: Draw a speech bubble with a tail pointing at anchor. Use an actor anchor like actor.top to place the bubble above the actor. Works with any AnchorPoint.
content.ref_say_param_anchor: Where the tail points. Use actor.top, actor.right, Window.center, etc.
content.ref_say_param_padding: Space between the text and bubble edge.
content.ref_text_size: Set the font size for text() calls.
content.ref_text_align: Set text alignment. Use "left", "center", or "right" for horizontal; "top", "middle", or "bottom" for vertical.
content.ref_image: Draw a sprite at position (x, y). `img` can be an asset dict from assets.sprites, a Sprite object (raw pixel buffer), a SpriteEntry from assets.sheet, or a SheetAnimation. Draws the top-left corner at (x, y). Pass w/h to scale; omit for natural size.
content.ref_image_advanced: When given a `SpriteEntry` or `SheetAnimation`, `image()` always draws frame 0 (the static default). To draw a specific frame use indexing: `image(assets.sheet.hero.idle[2], x, y)`. For animated Actors backed by a SpriteEntry, use AnimationController.tick() and Actor.draw() instead — those handle frame selection automatically.
content.ref_image_param_img: Asset dict, Sprite, SpriteEntry, or SheetAnimation.
content.ref_image_param_w: Draw width. Defaults to sprite's natural width.
content.ref_image_param_h: Draw height. Defaults to sprite's natural height.
content.ref_colors_palette: The locked Sweetie 16 palette (GrafxKid, CC0). Use anywhere a color is accepted. Same 16 names that appear in the sprite editor — pixels and code stay visually consistent.
content.ref_fill_color: Set the fill color. Accepts a color name string ("red"), a Colors.* tuple, three RGB numbers (0–255), a single gray value, or None to disable fill (same as no_fill()).
content.ref_fill_color_advanced: Fill is a *state machine*: once set, every subsequent shape uses this color until you change it. The state survives across `main()` calls within a frame but resets to its initial value at the start of every frame, so you must re-call `fill` each frame (or wrap it in `push`/`pop` if you only want the change to be local). `fill(None)` is identical to `no_fill()` — use whichever reads more naturally.
content.ref_fill_color_param_color: Color name, Colors.* value, RGB tuple, gray value, or None.
content.ref_no_fill: Disable fill so shapes are drawn as outlines only. fill(None) is a shorthand for the same effect.
content.ref_stroke_color: Set the outline color. Accepts a color name, a Colors.* tuple, three RGB values, or None to disable the outline (same as no_stroke()).
content.ref_stroke_color_advanced: Stroke is a state machine just like `fill`: persists across shapes within a frame, resets at the start of the next frame. Lines need *both* a stroke color and a non-zero `stroke_width` — setting only one of them silently produces nothing visible. `stroke(None)` is identical to `no_stroke()`.
content.ref_stroke_color_param_color: Color name, Colors.* value, RGB components, or None.
content.ref_no_stroke: Disable outline so shapes are drawn without borders. stroke(None) is a shorthand for the same effect.
content.ref_stroke_width: Set the thickness of outlines and lines in pixels.
content.ref_stroke_width_advanced: Width is integer-only — fractional values get truncated. It is *not* compensated for `scale()`, so a `stroke_width(2)` inside `scale(3)` draws as 6 screen pixels. Resets per frame like other state.
content.ref_lerp: Linear interpolation between two values. Works on numbers (positions, audio volumes, time) and on colors (RGB tuples, hex strings, or color names). Pick `t=0` for `a`, `t=1` for `b`, `t=0.5` for the midpoint. The same primitive transfers everywhere — it is the foundational tool.
content.ref_lerp_advanced: RGB interpolation by default — for two distant hues you get a *muddy middle* (e.g. red→green passes through brown), which is a teachable color-theory moment. If you want a more vibrant midpoint, lerp in HSL space yourself or compose with `saturated()`. For numbers, `lerp` does not clamp `t` to [0, 1] — values outside that range extrapolate beyond `a`/`b`, useful for overshoot effects.
content.ref_lerp_param_a: Start value — number or color (tuple, hex, or name).
content.ref_lerp_param_t: Position along the line: 0 = a, 1 = b, 0.5 = midpoint.
content.ref_lerp_returns: Number if `a` and `b` are numbers; an (r, g, b) tuple otherwise.
content.ref_darker: Return a darker shade of `color` by blending toward black. One step matches one stroke of the editor's darken brush, so pixel-art shading from code and from the editor stay visually consistent.
content.ref_darker_param_color: Color to darken (tuple, hex, or name).
content.ref_darker_param_steps: How many shade steps darker. Clamps so high values stop at pure black.
content.ref_lighter: Return a lighter shade of `color` by blending toward white. Mirror of `darker` — same step size as the editor's lighten brush.
content.ref_lighter_param_color: Color to lighten (tuple, hex, or name).
content.ref_lighter_param_steps: How many shade steps lighter. Clamps at pure white.
content.ref_saturated: Return a more vivid version of `color` by raising its HSL saturation. Use to punch a flat palette color into a highlight or focus accent.
content.ref_saturated_param_color: Color to saturate (tuple, hex, or name).
content.ref_saturated_param_steps: Steps more saturated. Clamps at fully saturated.
content.ref_desaturated: Return a duller version of `color` by lowering its HSL saturation. Push background colors toward gray so foreground actors read clearly.
content.ref_desaturated_param_color: Color to desaturate (tuple, hex, or name).
content.ref_desaturated_param_steps: Steps less saturated. Clamps at gray.
content.ref_sheet: Editor-authored pixel assets, exposed in Python as Sprite objects you can read, modify, and redraw. `sheet["hero"]` returns the Sprite for the asset called "hero". Mutations affect the in-Python copy only — the original asset on disk is unchanged.
content.ref_sheet_advanced: Sprites in `sheet` are populated when the program starts and are *copies* of the editor pixels, decoded from PNG/SVG via an OffscreenCanvas in the worker. Writes don't bleed back to the editor or the asset file. To draw the modified pixels, pass the Sprite to `image()` — the legacy `assets.sprites.hero` path still renders the unmodified original, by design. Looking up an unknown name raises `KeyError`.
content.ref_sheet_returns: The Sprite for the named asset.
content.ref_sprite_class: A rectangular RGBA pixel buffer. Returned by `create_sprite()`, `sheet["name"]`, and `assets.sheet.<sprite>.<anim>[n]`. Read dimensions with `.width`/`.height`, manipulate pixels with `get_pixel`/`set_pixel` or by iterating, and undo mutations with `.reset()`.
content.ref_sprite_class_advanced: Sprites hold a flat `bytearray` of length `width * height * 4` (RGBA order). `reset()` restores to the bytes captured at construction time — for `sheet[]` sprites that means the original editor pixels; for `create_sprite()` sprites it means the state at creation. Mutations (set_pixel, palette_swap, flood_fill, etc.) are in-place and cumulative; call `reset()` before re-running a procedural effect to avoid drift across frames.
content.ref_sprite_class_param_sprite.reset(): Restore all pixels to the state at construction time.
content.ref_sprite_class_param_for pixel in spri: Iterate every pixel left-to-right, top-to-bottom. Yields PixelView objects (see PixelView entry).
content.ref_create_sprite: Create a new blank Sprite — a rectangular RGBA pixel buffer that code can read and write pixel-by-pixel. With `fill`, every pixel starts at that color; without it, the sprite is fully transparent.
content.ref_create_sprite_advanced: Sprites are stored as a flat `bytearray` of length `width * height * 4` (RGBA). Reading or writing one pixel is O(1); a full sprite is O(width × height). Out-of-bounds reads return `None` and writes are silently ignored, so kids can draw in a loop without bounds checks. In Substage 1a sprites exist as pure data — the editor-asset path and canvas rendering land in Substage 1b.
content.ref_create_sprite_param_fill: Initial color for every pixel. None leaves the sprite fully transparent.
content.ref_get_pixel: Read a single pixel as an (r, g, b) tuple. Returns `None` for fully transparent pixels (alpha = 0) and for out-of-bounds coordinates — `if get_pixel(...) is None` is the kid-friendly transparency check.
content.ref_get_pixel_returns: (r, g, b) tuple, or None if transparent or out of bounds.
content.ref_set_pixel: Write a single pixel. `color` accepts the usual tuple/hex/name forms; pass `None` to erase (fully transparent). Out-of-bounds writes are silently ignored.
content.ref_set_pixel_advanced: Out-of-bounds tolerance is intentional: it lets kids write loops like `for x in range(-2, 12)` without crashing. If you need strict bounds, check `x < sprite.width` and `y < sprite.height` first. Writes always set alpha to 255 (opaque) — there is no per-pixel partial transparency in this version.
content.ref_set_pixel_param_color: Color to write, or None to erase.
content.ref_palette_swap: Replace every pixel of `old_color` with `new_color`. Exact RGB match — useful for color-as-data effects like player-controlled team colors, mood lighting, "press 1–9 to recolor my shirt." Pass `new_color=None` to erase matching pixels.
content.ref_palette_swap_param_old_color: Color to find (tuple, hex, or name).
content.ref_palette_swap_param_new_color: Replacement color, or None to erase.
content.ref_flood_fill: Bucket-fill connected pixels of the same color starting at (x, y). 4-connected (orthogonal); stops at any color change, including transparency boundaries. Same algorithm as the editor's bucket tool.
content.ref_flood_fill_param_color: Fill color, or None to erase.
content.ref_darken: Replace pixel (x, y) with `darker(pixel, steps)` — the in-place version of `darker`. Pair this with the editor's darken brush to teach the same shading technique in two media. No-op on transparent pixels and out-of-bounds coords.
content.ref_lighten: In-place version of `lighter`. Mirror of `darken` — same step size as the editor's lighten brush.
content.ref_saturate: In-place version of `saturated`. Punches a single pixel toward a more vivid version of its hue.
content.ref_desaturate: In-place version of `desaturated`. Pushes a single pixel toward gray.
content.ref_pixel_view: A mutable reference to a single pixel, yielded when you iterate a Sprite or an Actor. Read the color with pixel.color, write it with pixel.color = ... or pixel.set(color). Comparing with == checks the color value. Transparent pixels compare equal to None.
content.ref_pixel_view_advanced: IMPORTANT: `pixel = Colors.orange` only rebinds the loop variable and does NOT write back. Always use `pixel.color = ...` or `pixel.set(...)` to mutate the sprite. `.x` and `.y` are the pixel's column/row. Transparent pixels are returned by the iterator (`.color is None`); writing to them sets them opaque. On an Actor, iteration walks the default sprite frame (frame 0 of the first animation).
content.ref_pixel_view_param_pixel.color: (r, g, b) tuple, or None if transparent. Settable: pixel.color = Colors.red.
content.ref_pixel_view_param_pixel.set(color): Write a new color. Equivalent to pixel.color = color.
content.ref_pixel_view_param_pixel == color: Compare against any color form (tuple, hex, name, or None for transparent).
content.ref_push: Save the current drawing state (fill, stroke, transforms). Use with pop().
content.ref_push_advanced: `push()` snapshots the *whole* drawing state — the transform matrix plus fill/stroke/stroke-width — onto a stack. The matrix and color state reset to identity at the start of every frame, so unbalanced push/pop in one frame is only visible until the next `main()` tick. Nesting is fine, but each `push` must have a matching `pop` or later draws in the same frame use the wrong state.
content.ref_pop: Restore the drawing state saved with push().
content.ref_pop_advanced: `pop()` without a matching `push()` pops off the bottom of the stack — the result is undefined and downstream draws in that frame are likely wrong. The matrix always resets per-frame, so a single stray `pop` does not corrupt later frames, only the current one.
content.ref_translate: Move the drawing origin by (x, y). Shapes drawn after this will be shifted.
content.ref_translate_advanced: Translations accumulate: `translate(50, 0); translate(50, 0)` shifts a total of 100px. Order matters with `rotate`/`scale` — translate-then-rotate orbits drawing around `(x, y)`, while rotate-then-translate rotates the offset vector itself. Wrap a temporary translate in `push()`/`pop()` to keep it from leaking into the rest of the frame.
content.ref_rotate: Rotate the coordinate system by the given angle in degrees (clockwise).
content.ref_rotate_advanced: Rotation pivots around the *current origin* — to rotate around a point, `translate(x, y)` first so the origin is there, then draw the shape centered on `(0, 0)`. Angles accumulate, so `rotate(30); rotate(60)` equals one `rotate(90)`. Note that `rotate` only transforms the coordinate system: it has no effect on a Rect/Circle actor's collider, which stays axis-aligned in world coordinates.
content.ref_scale: Scale the drawing. Pass one value for uniform scale, or two for independent axes.
content.ref_scale_advanced: Scaling pivots around the current origin, so positions multiply along with sizes — `scale(2); rect(50, 50, …)` lands at `(100, 100)`. A negative factor flips the axis (`scale(-1, 1)` mirrors horizontally), which is the standard way to flip a sprite. Stroke width is *not* automatically corrected for scale: lines drawn after `scale(2)` are twice as thick on screen.
content.ref_scale_param_y: Vertical scale factor. Defaults to x.
content.ref_camera: A 2D camera offset. Use as a context manager — inside `with cam:` everything you draw is shifted so the camera's position appears at the center of the canvas. Combine with cam.follow(actor) for scrolling worlds.
content.ref_camera_param_Camera(x=0, y=0): Create a camera at world position (x, y).
content.ref_camera_param_Camera(actor): Shorthand for Camera().follow(actor) — create a camera that immediately tracks the given actor.
content.ref_camera_param_cam.follow(actor, lerp=: Make the camera track an actor each frame. lerp=1.0 snaps; values <1 smooth.
Inside the block, draw calls are shifted so the camera position lands at the canvas center.
content.ref_vector2: A 2D vector with arithmetic and geometry helpers. `Point` is an alias of `Vector2` — use whichever reads more naturally. Accepts numeric pairs, tuples, or other Vector2s in arithmetic. Mutable: you can assign to `.x` and `.y`.
content.ref_vector2_advanced: Vector2 is mutable but `+`, `-`, `*`, `/` all return *new* vectors — only `+=`/`-=` mutate in place. Equality is component-wise float comparison: `Vector2(0.1+0.2) == Vector2(0.3)` is `False` due to floating-point error — use `distance_to(...) < epsilon` for fuzzy checks. `normalized()` on the zero vector returns the zero vector (no division-by-zero, no exception). Arithmetic accepts `(x, y)` tuples on either side: `Vector2(1, 0) + (0, 1)` works.
content.ref_vector2_param_v + w / v - w / -v: Arithmetic with another Vector2 or a 2-tuple.
content.ref_vector2_param_v.normalized(): Unit vector in the same direction (zero vector stays zero).
content.ref_polar: Build a Vector2 from a magnitude and an angle in degrees. Angle convention matches actor.angle and actor.move(): 0° = east (+x), 90° = south (+y, screen y-down), 180° = west, 270° = north. The most common use is setting actor.vel for continuous motion at an angle without writing the trig yourself.
content.ref_polar_advanced: Polar returns a *new* Vector2 — there is no in-place version. The angle convention is counterclockwise in math but clockwise on screen because the canvas y axis points down, so `Polar(1, 90)` points down (south), not up. A negative magnitude is allowed and reverses the direction, equivalent to adding 180° to the angle.
content.ref_polar_param_magnitude: Length of the resulting vector (e.g. speed in pixels per frame).
content.ref_polar_param_angle_degrees: Direction in degrees. Pass actor.angle to match a sprite's facing.
content.ref_polar_param_Polar(120, 60): 120 px/frame at 60° (down-right). Assign to actor.vel for movement.
content.ref_polar_param_Polar(8, ship.angle): Bullet velocity that matches the ship's current facing.
content.ref_polar_returns: A new Vector2 of the given magnitude in the given direction.
content.ref_run: Start the game loop. The function main() is called every frame to draw and update your program. Also available as Window.run(main, fps).
content.ref_run_advanced: Each call to `run()` cancels any previously running loop and resets `frame_count` to 0 — calling it again restarts the game cleanly. Per-frame order is fixed: every living actor's `_apply_velocity()` (consuming `vx`/`vy`), then each actor's `update()`, then your `main()`. Key/mouse `pressed`/`released` flags are cleared at the *end* of each frame, so by the time the next frame starts they are False again unless the event repeats. `fps` only sets the *target* — heavy frames may take longer and your code should not assume a fixed dt.
content.ref_run_param_main: A function called each frame. No arguments.
content.ref_stop: Stop the game loop. Also available as Window.stop().
content.ref_frame_rate: Change the target frame rate while the game loop is running.
content.ref_frame_rate_advanced: Takes effect from the *next* scheduled tick, not the currently-pending one — calling `frame_rate(30)` inside `main()` keeps the current frame on its previous schedule. `frame_count` keeps counting at the new rate without resetting.
content.ref_frame_count: Read-only integer that counts how many frames have elapsed since the last run(). Starts at 0 and increments by 1 each frame. Useful for timing events: if frame_count % 60 == 0: ...
content.ref_frame_count_advanced: `frame_count` resets to 0 on every `run()`, so it counts *this* loop, not lifetime ticks. It increments *after* `main()` returns, so the first `main()` invocation sees `frame_count == 0`. Tying timing to `frame_count % N` couples your code to the current fps — switch to `Timer` (wall-clock) if you want behaviour stable across `frame_rate()` changes or stutter.
content.ref_timer: Wall-clock countdown timer. Poll t.done() (or t.left() <= 0) each frame, then call t.restart() to start the next interval. Frame-rate independent. Example: t = Timer(s=2); if t.done(): spawn(); t.restart()
content.ref_timer_advanced: Timer is wall-clock (`time.monotonic()`), so it ticks during stalls and across `frame_rate()` changes — use it whenever you want behaviour independent of fps. `done()` stays True until you call `restart()`, so without a restart the branch fires every frame after expiry. Constructing `Timer()` with no `s` or `ms` gives duration 0 — it's already done on frame 1; pair with `restart(s=…)` when you need a deferred first interval.
content.ref_timer_left: Seconds remaining. Negative when the timer has expired.
content.ref_timer_elapsed: Seconds since the timer was started or last restarted.
content.ref_timer_done: True when the interval has elapsed.
content.ref_timer_restart: Reset the timer's start point. Pass a new s or ms to also change the duration.
content.ref_sounds: Audio clips. Upload mp3/ogg/wav files in the Assets panel under the Sounds tab; access them as assets.sounds.<name>. Methods: play(), loop(), pause(), stop(). Each play() allocates a fresh stream, so overlapping plays work. Example: assets.sounds.pop.play()
content.ref_sound_play: Play the sound once from the start.
content.ref_sound_loop: Play the sound on repeat until stop() is called.
content.ref_sound_pause: Pause the most recently started instance of this sound.
content.ref_sound_stop: Stop every instance of this sound and reset playback.
content.ref_window_singleton: A singleton with canvas size, anchor points, and game-loop control. Window.width and Window.height always reflect the current canvas size — unlike width() and height(), they update immediately when the canvas is resized.
content.ref_window_anchors: AnchorPoints at screen edges and corners. Pass one to text() or say() for automatic edge-aligned placement with built-in padding. All positions update dynamically if the canvas is resized.
content.ref_window_anchors_param_Window.top_left: Top-left corner (text aligns left, baseline top).
content.ref_window_anchors_param_Window.top_righ: Top-right corner (text aligns right, baseline top).
content.ref_window_anchors_param_Window.bottom_l: Bottom-left corner (text aligns left, baseline bottom).
content.ref_window_anchors_param_Window.bottom_r: Bottom-right corner (text aligns right, baseline bottom).
content.ref_window_anchors_param_Window.left: Left center (text aligns right, baseline middle).
content.ref_window_anchors_param_Window.right: Right center (text aligns left, baseline middle).
content.ref_anchor_point: Represents a position with alignment hints. Returned by Window.<edge> and actor.<edge> properties. Pass it to text() or say(). x and y can be callables (for dynamic positions) or plain numbers.
content.ref_anchor_point_advanced: AnchorPoint subclasses Vector2, so it works in arithmetic, equality, and `distance_to`. `x` and `y` may be callables: `Window.top_right` stores lambdas that read the current canvas size, so the anchor re-resolves whenever the canvas resizes. Reading `.x`/`.y` evaluates the callable each access — cache it if you read repeatedly in one frame.
content.ref_anchor_point_param_x: X coordinate or a lambda returning it.
content.ref_anchor_point_param_y: Y coordinate or a lambda returning it.
content.ref_mouse: The current mouse state. Mouse.x/Mouse.y are the canvas coordinates. Mouse.down is true while a button is held, Mouse.pressed is true only on the first frame of a click, Mouse.released is true only on the frame the button is let go.
content.ref_mouse_advanced: `pressed` and `released` are frame-edge events: they read True for exactly one frame, then auto-clear at the end of that frame. Reading the same flag twice in one frame both return True, but only the *first* `main()` after the event sees it. There is no per-button distinction — `Mouse.down`/`pressed` fire for any button. `Mouse.x`/`Mouse.y` keep their last value between events; they are not `None` before the first mouse-move.
content.ref_mouse_param_Mouse.x: Current X position on the canvas.
content.ref_mouse_param_Mouse.y: Current Y position on the canvas.
content.ref_mouse_param_Mouse.down: True while any mouse button is held.
content.ref_mouse_param_Mouse.pressed: True only on the first frame of a click.
content.ref_mouse_param_Mouse.released: True only on the frame the button is released.
content.ref_keyboard: Check keyboard state. Access keys as attributes (Keyboard.space, Keyboard.arrow_left, Keyboard.a) or by string (Keyboard["1"]). Each key object has .down, .pressed, and .released.
content.ref_keyboard_advanced: Attribute and string access both raise on unknown keys (`AttributeError` and `KeyError` respectively) — there is no silent fallback. `pressed`/`released` clear at the end of every frame, so polling them mid-frame in two places sees the same edge twice within that frame. The OS key-repeat does *not* re-fire `pressed`: a held key emits one `pressed` and stays `down` until released. Reading a key object is cheap — `_Key` is constructed per access, no shared state.
content.ref_keyboard_param_.down: True while the key is held.
content.ref_keyboard_param_.pressed: True only on the first frame the key is pressed.
content.ref_keyboard_param_.released: True only on the frame the key is released.
content.ref_keyboard_keys: Arrow keys: arrow_left, arrow_right, arrow_up, arrow_down. Special: space, escape, enter, backspace, tab, shift, ctrl, alt. Letters: a–z. Number keys: key_0–key_9 (use the prefix because Keyboard.0 is not valid Python), or Keyboard["0"]–Keyboard["9"] with string syntax.
content.ref_keyboard_keys_advanced: `Keyboard.0` is a syntax error — Python identifiers cannot start with a digit. Use either `Keyboard.key_0` (the prefixed name) or `Keyboard["0"]` (string subscript). Name lookup is case-insensitive (`Keyboard.SPACE` works), and unknown names raise immediately rather than silently returning a dead key — so a typo surfaces in the console instead of producing a key that never fires.
content.ref_actor_class: Base class for game objects. Pass initial values as keyword arguments. Subclass it and define init() and/or update() to add custom behaviour.
content.ref_actor_class_advanced: Every Actor registers itself in `Actor.all_actors()` on construction — even an instance you never store in a variable still occupies a slot. Defining `init(self)` on a subclass runs it after kwargs are applied; defining `update(self)` makes the game loop call it before `main()` each frame. The `angle` setter wraps the value to [0, 360) automatically. Passing an asset (sprite/animation result) as the first positional arg auto-sets a rect collider matching its declared size — `Actor(assets.sprites.knight)` already has a hitbox.
content.ref_actor_class_param_angle: Rotation in degrees. Purely visual — affects draw() rotation and actor.move(distance). To move at an angle automatically, set actor.vel = Polar(speed, angle).
content.ref_actor_class_param_vx: Horizontal velocity (pixels per frame, applied automatically).
content.ref_actor_class_param_vy: Vertical velocity (pixels per frame, applied automatically).
content.ref_actor_class_param_pos: Position as a Vector2. Reading returns a fresh vector; assigning sets x and y. Useful for math: actor.pos += Vector2(0, 1).
content.ref_actor_class_param_vel: Velocity as a Vector2 (pairs with pos). Set with Polar(speed, angle) for movement at an angle: bullet.vel = Polar(8, ship.angle).
content.ref_actor_class_param_image: Sprite from assets.sprites, a SpriteEntry from assets.sheet, or any value accepted by image().
content.ref_actor_class_param_scale: Uniform draw scale. 2.0 draws at double size. Does not affect the collider.
content.ref_actor_class_param_flip_x: Mirror the sprite horizontally on draw.
content.ref_actor_class_param_flip_y: Mirror the sprite vertically on draw.
content.ref_actor_methods_advanced: `move(d)` uses the visual `angle`, not velocity — useful for one-shot imperative steps, but it ignores `vx/vy` completely. All movement methods short-circuit to a no-op after `die()`, so logic targeting a dead actor silently does nothing instead of erroring. `future_state` mirrors `_apply_velocity` exactly (single `vx, vy` step) and never mutates the actor, so calling `future_state.collides_any(...)` multiple times per frame is safe. `die()` removes the actor from `Actor._registry` immediately, but any reference held in a `Group` lingers until the next iteration over that group.
content.ref_actor_methods_param_move(distance): One-shot step: move forward by distance in the direction of angle (using the visual rotation). Useful when you want a per-frame imperative step instead of a continuous velocity. For continuous motion at an angle, set actor.vel = Polar(distance_per_frame, angle).
content.ref_actor_methods_param_change_x_by(dx): Add dx to the x position.
content.ref_actor_methods_param_change_y_by(dy): Add dy to the y position.
content.ref_actor_methods_param_rotate(degrees): Turn by the given number of degrees.
content.ref_actor_methods_param_draw(): Draw this actor on the canvas.
content.ref_actor_methods_param_update(): Called automatically each frame by the game loop before main(). Override in subclass to add per-actor logic without writing it inside main().
content.ref_actor_methods_param_die(): Remove this actor from the game.
content.ref_actor_methods_param_is_alive(): True if the actor has not been removed.
content.ref_actor_methods_param_reset(): Restore all sprite frames to their original pixel data (undoes any set_pixel / palette_swap / etc. mutations). Useful before re-applying a procedural effect each frame.
content.ref_actor_methods_param_for pixel in act: Iterate every pixel of the actor's default sprite frame, yielding PixelView objects you can read and write. Same as iterating the Sprite directly.
content.ref_actor_methods_param_collides_with(ot: True if this actor's collider overlaps other's. Both must have a collider configured.
content.ref_actor_methods_param_collides_any(gro: Returns the first actor in group this actor overlaps, or None.
content.ref_actor_methods_param_future_state: One-frame lookahead. actor.future_state.collides_any(walls) returns the wall the actor will hit next frame, without moving the actor. Use to stop motion before a collision: if player.future_state.collides_any(walls): player.vel = (0, 0).
content.ref_actor_collider: Each actor has a collider that defines its hitbox. Rect and Circle actors configure their colliders automatically. For a base Actor (or to override the shape), call set_circle or set_rect. Without a collider shape, collides_with always returns False.
content.ref_actor_collider_advanced: Without `set_circle` or `set_rect`, `collides_with` returns `False` and `collides_any` returns `None` — silent, not an error. Rect-vs-rect uses AABB testing in world coordinates: a visually rotated Rect still collides as if axis-aligned. Circle-vs-rect uses the exact closest-point test. The `dx/dy` offset lets the hitbox sit off-center from the sprite (e.g. at a character's feet), which also shifts where the anchor points land.
content.ref_actor_collider_param_collider.set_ci: Set a circular hitbox with radius r. dx/dy offset the hitbox from the actor's center.
content.ref_actor_collider_param_collider.set_re: Set a rectangular hitbox of size w×h. dx/dy offset the hitbox.
content.ref_actor_collider_param_collider.shape: "circle", "rect", or None when no hitbox is set.
content.ref_actor_collider_param_collider.active: The hitbox center, accounting for dx/dy offset.
content.ref_actor_collider_param_actor.collidabl: True if the collider has a shape set.
content.ref_actor_spatial: Helpers for placing and moving actors relative to the canvas boundaries.
content.ref_actor_spatial_advanced: `random_position()` reads the *collider* half-size to keep the body inside the canvas — a bare `Actor` with no collider falls back to margin 0 and can land touching any edge. `wrap_x`/`wrap_y` only correct for one canvas-width crossing per call, so an actor moving faster than the canvas width in a single frame will not snap correctly — clamp velocity instead. `in_bounds()` checks the actor's center only, not the full body; pair it with anchor points (`actor.left`, `actor.right`) if you need a full-body test.
content.ref_actor_spatial_param_random_position(: Teleport so the actor is fully inside the canvas. Uses the collider shape for margin (circle radius or half-rect size), so the actor never sticks out. Falls back to any position on a bare Actor.
content.ref_actor_spatial_param_wrap_x(): If the actor leaves the left or right edge, it appears on the opposite side.
content.ref_actor_spatial_param_wrap_y(): Same as wrap_x() but for top and bottom edges.
content.ref_actor_spatial_param_wrap(): Wrap in both directions at once.
content.ref_actor_spatial_param_in_bounds(): True if the actor's center is within the canvas (0 ≤ x ≤ width, 0 ≤ y ≤ height).
content.ref_actor_anchors: Each actor exposes AnchorPoints at its edges. Size precedence: an explicit collider (Circle radius, Rect half-size) wins; otherwise the actor's sprite (`image`) dimensions are used; a bare Actor with no image returns its center for all anchors. AnchorPoints behave as Vector2 (arithmetic, equality, distance_to), so you can pass them to tile_at() or do math directly.
content.ref_actor_anchors_advanced: AnchorPoint is a Vector2 subclass, so anchors participate in arithmetic, equality, and `distance_to` — pass `hero.top` straight into `tile_at()` or compute `enemy.center.distance_to(player.pos)`. Size precedence is collider → sprite `image` dimensions → zero, so a bare `Actor` with no collider and no image returns the actor's center for *every* anchor. Anchors are recomputed on each access, so they always reflect the actor's current position and the current collider offset (`dx`/`dy`).
content.ref_actor_anchors_param_actor.top: Top edge center. Use with say() or text() to place content above the actor.
content.ref_actor_static_param_Actor.all_actors(: Returns a list of every living actor.
content.ref_actor_static_param_Actor.random_coor: Returns a random (x, y) within the canvas (does not account for actor size). Prefer actor.random_position() when you want the full body inside the canvas.
content.ref_rect_actor: A rectangle actor that draws itself. Automatically sets a rect collider matching its size. The color parameter accepts a color name string, a Colors.* tuple, or an RGB tuple.
content.ref_rect_actor_advanced: The collider is auto-sized from the constructor `width`/`height` and is *not* updated if you later reassign `actor.width` — call `actor.collider.set_rect(w, h)` when the size changes at runtime. Visual `angle` rotates the drawn rectangle but not the collider, which stays axis-aligned in world coordinates. `color` and `stroke_color` accept a name string, a `Colors.*` tuple, or an RGB tuple interchangeably.
content.ref_rect_actor_param_color: Fill color (name, Colors.*, or RGB tuple).
content.ref_rect_actor_param_stroke_color: Outline color. No outline if omitted.
content.ref_circle_actor: A circle actor that draws itself. Automatically sets a circle collider with the given radius.
content.ref_circle_actor_advanced: The collider radius is fixed at construction; reassigning `actor.radius` later does not update the hitbox — call `actor.collider.set_circle(r)` when it changes at runtime. The circle collider is rotation-invariant, so `angle` has no effect on collisions (only on any sprite drawn on top). Setting `actor.image` is fine: the sprite is drawn at the same center, but the hitbox stays circular regardless of sprite shape.
content.ref_circle_actor_param_radius: Radius (also used as the collider radius).
content.ref_circle_actor_param_color: Fill color (name, Colors.*, or RGB tuple).
content.ref_circle_actor_param_stroke_color: Outline color. No outline if omitted.
content.ref_group: A collection of actors that is safe to iterate even while actors are dying. Dead actors are filtered out automatically on each iteration.
content.ref_group_advanced: Iteration filters dead actors lazily — passing through a Group cleans it up. `len(group)` is *not* filtered, so recently-dead actors still count until the next iteration sweep. `add()` does not deduplicate: adding the same actor twice gives it two slots and `collides_any` will test it twice. Iteration is safe during `add`/`remove`/`die` because `__iter__` returns a fresh list copy each time.
content.ref_group_param_add(actor): Add an actor to the group.
content.ref_group_param_remove(actor): Remove an actor from the group.
content.ref_group_param_len(group): Number of actors in the group (including recently dead ones until next iteration).
content.ref_group_param_if group:: True if the group has any actors. Use as a quick 'are there any enemies left?' check.
content.ref_assets_tilemaps: Access a project tilemap by name. Returns a TileMap object containing all of its layers. The tilemap must be created in the sprite editor and added to the project first.
content.ref_assets_tilemaps_param_name: Tilemap name as set in the editor, e.g. assets.tilemaps.level1.
content.ref_tilemap_class: A collection of named TilemapLayers drawn bottom-to-top. Call draw() each frame to render all layers at an offset — useful for scrolling.
content.ref_tilemap_class_advanced: Layers draw bottom-to-top in the order set by the editor, so a layer added later visually covers earlier ones — useful for foliage or rooftops on top of a ground layer. Attribute access falls through to `layers`: `level.background` is shorthand for `level.layers["background"]`, and raises `AttributeError` (not `KeyError`) on a missing layer. Areas are tilemap-wide — they don't belong to a layer — and are accessed under `level.areas.<name>` (see the Areas entry).
content.ref_tilemap_class_param_draw(x=0, y=0): Draw all layers at pixel offset (x, y). Tiles outside the canvas are skipped automatically.
content.ref_tilemap_class_param_layers: Dict of layer name → TilemapLayer. Access a specific layer with tilemap.layers["Layer 1"].
content.ref_tilemap_class_param_areas: Namespace of named cell-set zones brushed in the Tile Editor. `tilemap.areas.floor` returns a Group of merged-rect colliders for use with `actor.collides_any(...)`. See the "Areas" entry.
content.ref_tilemap_areas: Named cell-set zones brushed onto the tilemap in the Tile Editor. Each area becomes a Group of merged-rectangle colliders you can pass to `actor.collides_any(...)`. Use them for floors, walls, hazard zones, boss arenas — any region the game needs to test against. Areas are tilemap-wide; they do not belong to a specific layer.
content.ref_tilemap_areas_advanced: Adjacent cells in an area are greedily merged into rectangles when the tilemap loads, so a 30-cell wall stripe becomes one rectangle — `actor.collides_any` then runs against a handful of colliders instead of hundreds. The merge happens once at construction; areas are not editable from Python at runtime. Area names are validated in the editor as snake_case (`[a-z][a-z0-9_]*`) so `level.areas.<name>` always works as attribute access. An area you never brushed any cells into is a valid empty Group — safe to iterate. The TileRef actors inside the Group skip `Actor.all_actors()` — they exist only as collision shapes; the tilemap itself draws the pixels.
content.ref_tilemap_layer_class: A single named layer from a TileMap. Contains a sparse grid of tile names mapped to ImageBitmaps from the project assets. You can draw individual layers and query tiles by position.
content.ref_tilemap_layer_class_advanced: Cells are stored sparsely as a `dict[col][row]`, so an empty grid takes near-zero memory and `tile_at` on an empty cell returns `None` instead of erroring. `tile_at` accepts either two numbers or any single Vector2/Point/AnchorPoint — `layer.tile_at(player.bottom)` is the foot-on-floor check pattern. For collision queries, use tilemap-wide Areas (`tilemap.areas.<name>`) rather than walking individual layers — Areas come pre-merged into rectangles.
content.ref_tilemap_layer_class_param_draw(x=0,: Draw this layer at pixel offset (x, y).
content.ref_tilemap_layer_class_param_tile_at(px: Return the tile name at pixel position (px, py), or None if empty. Also accepts a single Vector2/Point/AnchorPoint: tile_at(player.bottom).
content.ref_tilemap_layer_class_param_get_tile(c: Return the tile name at grid column/row, or None if empty.
content.ref_tilemap_layer_class_param_tiles(): Yield (col, row, name) for every filled cell in the layer.
content.ref_tilemap_layer_class_param_name: The layer's name as set in the editor.
content.ref_tilemap_layer_class_param_tile_size: Tile size in pixels (all tiles in a layer are the same size).
content.ref_tilemap_layer_mutation: Mutate a tilemap layer from code. `set` writes a tile (pass `name=None` to clear); `get` returns `(name, rotation)` or `None`; `count_neighbors` returns how many of the 8 neighbors hold the given tile name — handy for cellular-automata cave generation.
content.ref_tilemap_layer_mutation_advanced: `rotation` must be one of {0, 90, 180, 270}; other values are reduced modulo 360. Out-of-map neighbors count as 0, so edge cells behave predictably in CA loops. The editor only writes rotation 0; non-zero rotations come from code. Mutations persist across frames within a run but are not written back to the saved tilemap file.
content.ref_tilemap_layer_mutation_param_name: Tile name to write, or None to clear.
content.ref_tilemap_group: Return a `TileGroup` over the named area. Unlike `level.areas.<name>` (which is collision-only), a TileGroup exposes cells, bounds, set transforms (shrink, border) and write helpers (fill, scatter, fill_random) — the vocabulary needed for procedural level building.
content.ref_tilemap_group_advanced: A TileGroup obtained via `level.group(name)` is bound to the first layer for mutation. With multiple layers, use `level.layers["foreground"].group(name)` to mutate a specific layer. Group transforms return new groups (no mutation); only `fill`, `scatter`, and `fill_random` write to the layer.
content.ref_tilemap_group_returns: A new TileGroup over the area's cells.
content.ref_tile_group: A set of (col, row) cells from a tilemap layer. Inspect with `cells()` (yields `Cell(x, y)` namedtuples), `bounds()` (returns `Bounds(min, max, width, height)`), `random_cell()`; transform into new groups with `shrink(n)` (4-connected erosion) and `border()` (cells with at least one missing 4-neighbor); write to the bound layer with `fill(name)`, `scatter(name, count=N)`, and `fill_random(choices, rotate=False)`.
content.ref_tile_group_advanced: `fill_random` accepts a list (uniform pick) or a dict `{name: weight}` for weighted distributions. `rotate=True` writes a random rotation in {0, 90, 180, 270} per cell — combine with a symmetric base tile for variety without per-tile art. `shrink(n)` applies erosion n times; `border()` is idempotent. All transforms are immutable: chain them freely (`g.shrink(1).border().fill(...)`).
content.ref_assets_overview: Top-level object populated at run-start with everything the project has authored. Five namespaces: assets.sprites (PNG/SVG images), assets.sheet (sheet sprites with animations), assets.sounds (audio clips), assets.tilemaps (tile maps), assets.animations (frame-strip animations). Accessing an unknown name raises AttributeError.
content.ref_assets_overview_param_assets.sprites: PNG/SVG image assets. See assets.sprites entry.
content.ref_assets_overview_param_assets.sheet: Sheet sprites with named animations. See assets.sheet entry.
content.ref_random_fn: Return a random float. With one argument, returns a value in [0, low). With two arguments, returns a value in [low, high).
content.ref_random_fn_advanced: Returns a `float` (uses `random.uniform`), not an integer — wrap with `int()` if you need a whole number. There is no seed control here; results are non-deterministic across runs. Both endpoints can appear in the result (uniform is inclusive on both sides for floats), unlike `random.randrange`.
content.ref_random_fn_param_low: Lower bound (or upper bound if high is omitted).
content.ref_noise: Smooth value noise in [0, 1]. Deterministic per (x, y, scale, seed) — call it twice with the same arguments and you get the same number. Use it to build natural-looking terrain heights, cave masks, or dithered colors.
content.ref_noise_advanced: Higher `scale` zooms in (smoother, slower features); lower `scale` zooms out (more rapid variation). For cave-like masks, `scale=0.1–0.3` and threshold around 0.5 works well. Change `seed` for a fresh world; the same seed always yields the same layout, so kids can share interesting seeds.
content.ref_random_color: Return a random color tuple from the Colors palette. The returned value can be passed directly to fill(), stroke(), or background().
content.ref_assets_sprites: Access a project sprite by filename without extension. The sprite must be added to the project first via the Assets panel.
content.ref_assets_sprites_advanced: Sprite assets are loaded asynchronously: until `done=True`, `image(...)` silently draws nothing — your code can reference a sprite at startup without erroring while the bitmap is still decoding. Names come from filenames, so renaming the asset in the editor breaks the reference.
content.ref_assets_sprites_param_name: Filename without extension, e.g. assets.sprites.ship for ship.svg.
content.ref_assets_animations: Access a project animation by name. Returns an Animation object whose frames are the drawings from the Animations panel. Call update() each frame and draw animation.frame with image().
content.ref_assets_animations_param_name: Animation name as set in the Animations panel, e.g. assets.animations.walk.
content.ref_animation_class: A frame-cycling sprite animation. Pass a list of sprite frames and the playback speed. Call update() every frame to advance the timer, then draw animation.frame with image(). Create animations in the Animations panel — they load automatically as assets.animations.<name>.
content.ref_animation_class_advanced: Animation `fps` is clamped to at least 1 frame per game tick — setting `fps` higher than the loop's target fps cannot make the animation play faster than one new sprite per tick. Each Animation has its own internal tick accumulator, so multiple Animations stay in sync individually even if the loop drops a frame. The `frames` list is *not* defensively copied at every access — mutating it externally affects the running animation.
content.ref_animation_class_param_frames: List of sprite frames (e.g. from assets.animations.walk.frame or custom list).
content.ref_animation_class_param_fps: Playback speed in frames per second. Also writable as anim.fps = 12 at any time.
content.ref_animation_update: Advance the animation timer by one game frame. Must be called once per frame inside main() to move between sprite frames.
content.ref_animation_update_advanced: `update()` is a no-op when the animation has 0 or 1 frame or is paused. If you forget to call it, `animation.frame` stays pinned on the same sprite forever (no error). Multiple calls per frame advance the animation that many ticks — useful for fast-forwarding, but the usual pattern is exactly one call per frame.
content.ref_animation_frame: The current sprite frame. Pass directly to image() to draw it. Returns None if the animation has no frames.
content.ref_animation_play: Control playback. play() resumes, pause() freezes on the current frame, reset() jumps back to frame 0 and resumes.
content.ref_animation_loop: Whether the animation loops back to frame 0 after the last frame. Set to False to hold on the last frame when done.
content.ref_animation_done: True when a non-looping animation has finished playing and is holding on the last frame.
content.ref_animation_done_advanced: `done` requires *all three*: `loop=False`, playback stopped, *and* the last frame reached. A looping animation always returns False. Calling `reset()` flips `done` back to False and starts playback again from the first frame.
content.ref_light_class: A multiply-blended lighting overlay with optional shadow-casting point sources. Create one Light per scene, add obstacle actors and light-source actors, call draw() last each frame so it composites over everything else.
content.ref_light_class_advanced: `mode='hsl'` (default) composites the lightmap with `soft-light` — perceptually closer to per-pixel lightness; `mode='overlay'` is a simpler alpha-blend. Visibility polygons for shadow-casting are cached and only recomputed when a source or obstacle moves. For a fully static scene the per-frame cost is O(sources + obstacles). Call `draw()` *after* all other drawing — it composites over whatever is on the canvas.
content.ref_light_class_param_ambient: Background light color (r, g, b). Low values make unlit areas very dark; (0,0,0) gives pure black outside light radius.
content.ref_light_class_param_radius: Default light source radius in pixels.
content.ref_light_add_obstacles: Register actors as light-blocking obstacles for shadow computation. Accepts a single Actor, a Group, a tilemap area, or any iterable of actors. Each actor's collider rectangle is used as the occluder shape.
content.ref_light_add_obstacles_advanced: Actors without a collider are silently skipped. Each call to `add_obstacles` invalidates the polygon cache — if you add many obstacles at once, pass a list or Group so the cache is invalidated only once.
content.ref_light_add_source: Add a point light source. Accepts an Actor (position tracks the actor each frame), a Vector2, or a (x, y) tuple (fixed position). Multiple sources supported.
content.ref_light_add_source_param_src: The light source position or actor to follow.
content.ref_light_shade: Set the color tint of light cones. Available names: 'neutral' (pure white), 'warm' (candlelight orange), 'cool' (blue daylight), 'moonlight' (pale blue), 'candle' (deep amber). Chainable.
content.ref_light_flicker: Enable a subtle deterministic intensity flicker [0.85–1.0] per light source, simulating a torch or candle. Uses frame_count and a per-Light seed so multiple lights flicker independently. Chainable.
content.ref_light_flicker_param_enabled: True to enable flicker, False to disable.
content.ref_light_radius_method: Change the light source radius after construction. Chainable.
content.ref_light_draw: Emit the lighting overlay. Must be called **last** each frame — after all background, tilemap, and actor draws — so it composites correctly over the full scene.
content.ref_assets_sheet_namespace: Namespace of named sprites from the project sheet. Access a sprite by attribute name: `assets.sheet.hero` returns the `SpriteEntry` for the sprite called "hero". Raises `AttributeError` with available names if the sprite doesn't exist.
content.ref_assets_sheet_namespace_advanced: `assets.sheet` is populated at run-start from the project sheet canvas. Each sprite entry's frames are extracted eagerly into individual `Sprite` objects so that Python code can read and modify pixels without per-frame decoding. If the project has no sheet, `assets.sheet` is an empty namespace — accessing any name raises `AttributeError`.
content.ref_sprite_entry: A named sprite from the sheet. Access animations by attribute: `assets.sheet.hero.idle` returns the `SheetAnimation` for the "idle" animation. When passed directly to `image()` or used as an `Actor` image, renders frame 0 of the first animation.
content.ref_sprite_entry_advanced: Accessing an unknown animation name raises `AttributeError` listing the available names. `SpriteEntry._default_sprite()` is used internally by `Actor.draw()` and `image()` when no animation controller has been ticked.
content.ref_sheet_animation: An animation strip: an ordered list of `Sprite` frames. Index it with `[n]` to get a specific frame; indexing wraps with modulo so `anim[frameCount]` is the same as `anim[0]`. `len(anim)` returns the number of frames. When passed to `image()`, renders frame 0.
content.ref_animation_controller_tick: Advance one frame of the named animation. Call once per game frame inside `update()` or `main()`. On the first tick, or after switching from a different animation, the frame resets to 0 (no advance this tick). On subsequent ticks of the same animation, the frame counter increments and wraps at `frameCount`. Calling `tick()` twice in the same frame prints a warning.
content.ref_animation_controller_tick_advanced: `actor.idle` returns an `AnimationController` bound to that actor instance — two actors can play the same animation at different frame positions. The controller is lazily created on first access and cached in `actor._anim_controllers`. The frame guard (`_ticked_this_frame`) is reset by `actor.draw()` so the next frame's `tick()` works normally. `ctrl.frame_idx` is readable (int) — useful for debug display or save/restore; it is not directly settable.
content.ref_actor_with_sheet: Create an actor whose image is a sheet sprite. Access animation controllers via attribute lookup (`actor.idle`, `actor.run`) — these return `AnimationController` objects. Call `.tick()` on the active animation each frame, then call `actor.draw()` to render the current frame centered on the actor's position.
content.ref_actor_with_sheet_advanced: Switching animations (calling `self.run.tick()` after `self.idle.tick()` was active) resets the new animation's frame to 0 on the first tick — the first frame of the new animation always shows for a full frame, preventing one-frame glitches. If no `.tick()` has been called yet, `draw()` renders frame 0 of the first animation as a static fallback.
content.concept_assets_body: An asset is a piece of content you load into your project from the Assets panel — a sprite, an animation, a tilemap, or a sound. Once uploaded, you access it from code through the global `assets` namespace by the name you gave it.
content.concept_coords_body: The canvas uses pixel coordinates. By default (0, 0) is the top-left corner; x grows to the right, y grows downward. Most things you draw have an anchor — the point on the shape that lines up with the (x, y) you give. For shapes it's usually the center; for images it's the top-left unless you change it.
content.concept_game_loop_body: A game is a loop: many times per second the program clears the screen, updates the state (positions, timers, input), and draws a new frame. Pass `run()` a function you want to call ~60 times a second. It's common to name this function `main` and have it call smaller functions in order — one for drawing, one for input, one for physics, and so on. Variables you want to keep between frames live outside the function.
content.concept_vectors_body: A position is two numbers (x, y). A velocity is also two numbers — how much x and y change each frame. To move something, add its velocity to its position every frame. `Vector2` packages both into one value so you can add, scale, or rotate them in one step.
content.concept_animation_concepts_body: An animation is a list of frames. Playing it means advancing through the frames over time. Frame rate (frames per second) controls speed. A looping animation goes back to the start when it ends; a non-looping one stops on the last frame. You drive an animation by calling `.update()` each frame.
content.concept_collisions_body: A collision is two shapes overlapping. The simplest check is bounding-box overlap (do two rectangles touch?). Actors get this for free via a `Collider`. Detection only tells you a collision happened — to stop the actor, you also need to *resolve* it (push it back out).
content.concept_transforms_body: `translate`, `rotate`, and `scale` change the coordinate system for everything drawn after them. They stack: `push()` saves the current transform, `pop()` restores it. The order matters — `translate` then `rotate` rotates around the moved origin, not the canvas origin. Use push/pop around any local transform to keep it from leaking into other drawings.
